description: Grupo de estudiantes del ISFT 151 y miembros de mardelplata.dev
summary: FieldShift DSS is an interactive, farmer-centered Decision Support System that turns NASA Earth observation datasets into actionable, multi-year crop rotation plans. Farmers manage heterogeneous parcels, such as sandy ridges and deep loams, under volatile rainfall, heat waves, and frost risk, yet orbital sensors operate at coarse resolutions (9-50 km) that cannot see individual field boundaries or subsurface soil chemistry. FieldShift DSS bridges this scale gap by fusing 15 years of historical NASA POWER weather data and NASA SMAP soil moisture estimates with parcel-level soil textures and optional local laboratory tests (Bray-1 Phosphorus and pH). Instead of outputting a single opaque recommendation, the platform simulates competing rotation strategies across real historical climate realizations to expose downside risk (P10), median outcomes (P50), and bare-soil exposure, empowering farmers and agronomists to stress-test climate scenarios and export a field-ready verification roadmap.
details:
The Challenge

Choosing a multi-year crop rotation requires balancing immediate cash flow against drought resilience, soil organic matter, and erosion control. Traditional agronomic calculators either rely on static regional averages that hide extreme drought/frost downside or assume uniform soil conditions across an entire farm. Conversely, raw satellite datasets leave farmers guessing how a 9 km soil moisture pixel or a 50 km meteorological grid cell translates to a 65-hectare sandy ridge versus an adjacent 80-hectare lowland parcel.

How FieldShift DSS Works

FieldShift DSS evaluates 4-season crop sequences across a multi-parcel farm portfolio using a pure parametric agro-hydrological surrogate engine:

  • Multi-Field Satellite Parcel Editor: Users pan across high-resolution satellite imagery (with regional presets across humid, subhumid, and semiarid zones) to place, resize, rotate, and configure up to four parcels overlaid directly against a native 9 km × 9 km NASA SMAP pixel footprint.
  • Probabilistic Risk Engine (P10–P50–P90): Compares three distinct strategies—Baseline (Current Rotation), Water-Resilient Rotation, and Regenerative & Soil Cover—across 15 historical NASA growing seasons, displaying uncertainty fan charts for total gross margin (USD), residual root-zone moisture (mm), and structural soil health.
  • Normalized Farmer Priorities: Hybrid sliders and exact numeric inputs let producers weight Water Stability & Downside Protection, Soil Health & Cover Continuity, and Short-Term Gross Margin, dynamically re-ranking strategies to match their risk tolerance.
  • "What-If" Climate Stress-Testing: Interactive perturbation controls let users simulate drier/wetter rainfall anomalies (-35% to +35%) and mean temperature warming (+0.0 °C to +3.5 °C) to see how each rotation holds up under future climate shifts.
  • Local Ground-Truthing & Spatial Honesty: Farmers can input field-sampled Bray-1 Phosphorus (ppm) and soil pH per parcel to calibrate legume nodulation and nutrient penalties, while the dashboard explicitly flags sub-pixel spatial uncertainty when total farm area is smaller than a single SMAP pixel.
  • Side-by-Side Scenario Comparator & Action Roadmap: Users can save multiple simulation snapshots, compare any two scenarios side-by-side (auditing net deltas and parcel-level crop changes), and export a Markdown Agronomic Action Roadmap containing a field scouting and soil sampling checklist.

How We Used NASA Data

  • NASA POWER Project (2011–2025): Fetches daily and growing-season meteorological time series for any selected parcel coordinates, including bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCOR), 2-meter maximum and minimum temperatures (T2M_MAX, T2_MIN) to compute heat (>34 °C) and agronomic frost (≤2 °C) stress days, and root-zone soil wetness (GWETROOT) to synchronize initial moisture reserves. An offline-safe historical cache guarantees uninterrupted operation during field demos.
  • NASA SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive): Provides baseline root-zone soil moisture context and visualizes the native 9 km × 9 km SMAP footprint directly over user-drawn field polygons so producers can inspect sub-pixel heterogeneity across ridges and lowlands.
  • Multi-Resolution Harmonization & Biophysical Rules: Regional NASA climate forcing is downscaled to each parcel using texture-specific effective rainfall retention multipliers (sandy, deep loam, clay, degraded), FAO-56 crop water demand coefficients, botanical family monoculture penalties (-15%), legume/cover-crop biological nitrogen credits (+12%), and a 12-month living-cover calendar tracking bare-soil erosion windows.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software

  • Frontend & Language: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • Geospatial & Data Visualization: Leaflet, React-Leaflet, Esri World Imagery & Reference Layers, Recharts (composed uncertainty fan charts)
  • Architecture & Persistence: Pure functional domain simulation engine decoupled from UI state, browser localStorage simulation history repository, and client-side Markdown report generation

Impact & Benefits

  • Quantifies Downside Protection: Shows farmers not just average expected profit, but how much financial loss is avoided during severe drought or frost years (P10 floor) by matching drought-tolerant crops like sorghum and sunflower to low-retention soils.
  • Reduces Bare-Soil Erosion Windows: Highlights months with low vegetation cover and demonstrates how winter cover crops (Vetch + Rye) protect topsoil and fix biological nitrogen prior to extractive cereals.
  • Human-in-the-Loop Design: Treats satellite data as a decision aid rather than an oracle, explicitly listing what orbital sensors cannot observe (subsurface compaction, weed seedbanks, uncalibrated soil pH/phosphorus) and generating a concrete verification order for the local agronomist.

Scientific References

  • Allen, R. G., Pereira, L. S., Raes, D., & Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration - Guidelines for computing crop water requirements (FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56). Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
  • Crookston, R. K., Kurle, J. E., Copeland, P. J., Ford, J. H., & Lueschen, W. E. (1991). Rotational cropping sequence affects yield of corn and soybean. Agronomy Journal, 83(1), 108–113.
  • Tonitto, C., David, M. B., & Drinkwater, L. E. (2006). Replacing bare fallows with cover crops in fertilizer-intensive cropping systems: A meta-analysis of crop yield and N dynamics. Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, 112(1), 58–72.
